summary.text: Fermat’s theorem reduces divisibility by each prime \(p<1399\) to a finite periodic computation of \(2^{58n+26}\bmod (p-1)\); all resulting residues are nonzero, except possible classes for \(p=67,271,523\), and those classes force coverage by one of the three earlier conjectures. Finally, \(2^{58n+26}\equiv204\pmod{233}\), together with \(2^{233}\equiv1\pmod{1399}\) and \(4\cdot2^{204}+3\equiv0\pmod{1399}\), proves divisibility by \(1399\), so excluding every smaller prime makes it the least prime factor.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(k)=2^{2^k+2}+3
\]
and let \(a(k)\) denote the least prime factor of \(F(k)\).  Fix \(n\geq 0\), and put
\[
k=58n+26,\qquad N=F(k)=2^{2^{58n+26}+2}+3.
\]
We assume throughout that \(k\) is not covered by any of the first three conjectures. Explicitly, this means that none of the following holds:

\[
\begin{array}{ll}
(C1)& k=10m+2\quad\hbox{for some }m\geq0,\\
(C2)& k=36m+16\quad\hbox{for some }m\geq0\hbox{ with }m\not\equiv1\pmod5,\\
(C3)& k=84m+22\quad\hbox{for some }m\geq0\hbox{ with }m\not\equiv0\pmod5.
\end{array}
\]

We shall prove first that \(1399\mid N\), and then that no prime less than \(1399\) divides \(N\).

## 1. The divisor 1399

The following four modular residues are obtained by repeated squaring:
\[
2^{26}\equiv204\pmod {233},\qquad
2^{58}\equiv1\pmod {233},
\]
\[
2^{233}\equiv1\pmod {1399},\qquad
4\cdot2^{204}+3\equiv0\pmod {1399}.
\]
(The same elementary modular calculation also shows that \(1399\) is prime; for example, one may trial-divide by the primes at most \(\sqrt{1399}<38\).)

The first two congruences imply, for every \(n\geq0\),
\[
2^{58n+26}=2^{26}(2^{58})^n\equiv204\pmod {233}.
\]
Thus there is an integer \(q\geq0\) such that
\[
2^{58n+26}=233q+204.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
N
 &=4\cdot2^{2^{58n+26}}+3\\
 &=4\cdot2^{233q+204}+3\\
 &=4(2^{233})^q2^{204}+3\\
 &\equiv4\cdot2^{204}+3\equiv0\pmod {1399}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Hence
\[
1399\mid N. \tag{1}
\]

## 2. A uniform reduction for primes below 1399

Let \(p\) be an odd prime. Define a sequence of residues modulo \(p-1\) by
\[
e_0=2^{26}\bmod(p-1),
\]
\[
e_{i+1}=e_i\bigl(2^{58}\bmod(p-1)\bigr)\bmod(p-1).
\]
A direct induction gives
\[
e_i\equiv2^{58i+26}\pmod {p-1},\qquad 0\leq e_i<p-1. \tag{2}
\]
Indeed, this is clear at \(i=0\), and multiplication by \(2^{58}\) proves the induction step.

By Fermat's theorem, \(2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p\). Therefore exponents of \(2\) may be reduced modulo \(p-1\), and (2) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
F(58i+26)
 &=4\cdot2^{2^{58i+26}}+3\\
 &\equiv4\cdot2^{e_i}+3\pmod p. \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]
Write
\[
v_i(p)=\bigl(4\cdot2^{e_i}+3\bigr)\bmod p.
\]
Thus \(p\mid F(58i+26)\) if and only if \(v_i(p)=0\).

There is also a simple way to turn this into a finite calculation. If for some positive integer \(P\) one has
\[
e_P=e_0, \tag{4}
\]
then the recurrence defining \(e_i\) is deterministic, so induction gives
\[
e_{i+P}=e_i
\]
for every \(i\), and hence both \(e_i\) and \(v_i(p)\) depend only on \(i\bmod P\). It is therefore enough to calculate the \(P\) values with \(0\leq i<P\).

We now record the entire finite calculation used below. In the following table an entry \(p:P\) means that (4) holds for that \(P\), and that direct iteration of the displayed recurrences gives
\[
v_i(p)\ne0\qquad(0\leq i<P), \tag{5}
\]

More precisely, direct iteration proves
\[
v_i(67)\ne0\quad\text{for }0\leq i<5\text{ with }i\ne2,
\]
\[
v_i(271)\ne0\quad\text{for }0\leq i<18\text{ with }i\ne11,
\]
and
\[
v_i(523)\ne0\quad\text{for }0\leq i<42\text{ with }i\ne26.
\]
No assertion about the omitted residue is needed here.

For completeness, trial division of the integers from \(3\) through \(1398\) shows that the 220 first coordinates in the table are precisely all the odd primes below \(1399\). Compositeness is checked by exhibiting a divisor no larger than the square root, and primality by checking that no prime no larger than the square root divides. Thus the table, together with the separate treatment of \(2\) below, covers every possible prime less than \(1399\).

We next explain why the three exceptional residue classes in (6) are impossible under our hypotheses.

## 3. The exceptional residue classes imply coverage

### The prime 67

Suppose \(n\equiv2\pmod5\), and write \(n=5q+2\). Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
58n+26
 &=58(5q+2)+26\\
 &=290q+142\\
 &=10(29q+14)+2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(k\) is covered by \((C1)\). Since \(k\) is assumed not to be covered by \((C1)\), we have
\[
n\not\equiv2\pmod5.
\]
The period-five calculation for \(67\) therefore gives \(v_n(67)\ne0\), and (3) shows
\[
67\nmid N. \tag{7}
\]

### The prime 271

Suppose \(n\equiv11\pmod {18}\), and write \(n=18q+11\). Put
\[
m=29q+18.
\]
A direct expansion gives
\[
58n+26=36m+16. \tag{8}
\]
There are two cases.

If \(m\not\equiv1\pmod5\), equation (8) says exactly that \(k\) is covered by \((C2)\).

If \(m\equiv1\pmod5\), write \(m=5t+1\). Then
\[
36m+16=36(5t+1)+16=180t+52=10(18t+5)+2,
\]
so \(k\) is covered by \((C1)\).

Thus \(n\equiv11\pmod {18}\) always forces coverage by either \((C1)\) or \((C2)\). Under our assumptions,
\[
n\not\equiv11\pmod {18}.
\]
The period-eighteen calculation for \(271\) and (3) now give
\[
271\nmid N. \tag{9}
\]

### The prime 523

Suppose \(n\equiv26\pmod {42}\), and write \(n=42q+26\). Put again
\[
m=29q+18.
\]
Expansion gives
\[
58n+26=84m+22. \tag{10}
\]
If \(m\not\equiv0\pmod5\), (10) says that \(k\) is covered by \((C3)\).

If \(m\equiv0\pmod5\), write \(m=5t\). Then
\[
84m+22=420t+22=10(42t+2)+2,
\]
so \(k\) is covered by \((C1)\).

Thus the exceptional congruence \(n\equiv26\pmod {42}\) forces coverage by either \((C1)\) or \((C3)\). Hence our assumptions imply
\[
n\not\equiv26\pmod {42},
\]
and the period-forty-two calculation for \(523\), together with (3), yields
\[
523\nmid N. \tag{11}
\]

## 4. Excluding every prime below 1399

First, \(N\) is odd: its first summand is a positive power of \(2\), hence even, while \(3\) is odd. Therefore
\[
2\nmid N. \tag{12}
\]

Now let \(p<1399\) be any odd prime. It appears in the finite table. If \(p\notin\{67,271,523\}\), let \(P\) be the period displayed beside it. For \(r=n\bmod P\), periodicity gives
\[
e_n=e_r,
\]
and the finite nonvanishing test (5) gives \(v_r(p)\ne0\). Hence \(v_n(p)\ne0\), and (3) shows that \(p\nmid N\).

For \(p=67,271,523\), the same conclusion follows respectively from (7), (9), and (11), because the only residue class not covered by the corresponding finite nonvanishing test has already been ruled out by the noncoverage assumptions.

Together with (12), this proves
\[
p\nmid N\qquad\text{for every prime }p<1399. \tag{13}
\]

## 5. Identification of the least prime factor

Certainly \(N>1\). Its least prime factor is itself a prime divisor of \(N\). By (13), that least prime factor cannot be below \(1399\), so
\[
a(58n+26)\geq1399.
\]
On the other hand, (1) says that \(1399\) divides \(N\), so the least prime factor of \(N\) is at most \(1399\). Therefore
\[
a(58n+26)=1399.
\]

This holds for every \(n\geq0\) for which the index \(58n+26\) is not covered by any of Conjectures 1–3, as required.
